newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina's Menem under fire for dismissing unrest.
newsitem.headline: Argentina's Menem under fire for dismissing unrest.

text.p: Argentine President Carlos Menem came under fire on Thursday for dismissing protests against unemployment and poverty in recent weeks.

Churchmen, political opponents and even members of his own Peronist Party criticised Menem for responding to a Catholic bishop on Wednesday by asking "Where are there people dying of hunger in Argentina?"

The bishop of the poor northwestern province of Jujuy, hit by more than 20 roadblocks by desperate unemployed sugar and steel workers, told the president to "get in touch with reality and listen to the people."

"I invite him to walk around the towns here ... and then speak. I don't know where he is looking but experience tells me there are a lot of people going hungry," said Monsignor Marcelo Palentin, who mediated between the protesters and local government to avoid more clashes with police.
The protests in Jujuy were not staged by unions or parties but by the jobless in towns where unemployment is as high as 40 percent, compared with the national 17.3 percent.

Protests started in April in the southern province of Neuquen, then popped up in Salta, Jujuy and Cordoba. They appeared to end after promises of jobs last week but erupted again this week in Corrientes, Misiones, Tucuman and Rosario.

The breadth and violence of the protests overshadowed some good news on foreign investment and underscored the gap between strong economic growth and the failure to cope with unemployment, just six percent when Menem took power in 1989.

Menem blames it all on "subversives" and has called on businessmen who have benefited from the new stability to help create jobs. But his former deputy and likely successor as the Peronist candidate in 1999's presidential race, Buenos Aires province Gov. Eduardo Duhalde, contradicted him.

"It is the state that must help the poor -- like I am doing in my province," Duhalde said. "We cannot speak of an outbreak of subversion. Democracy is sometimes expressed by extreme protests but we should not be scared by that."

Duhalde, who portrays himself as closer to the ideals of party founder Juan Peron than Menem, said the 3,000 children needing assistance in his province every year "don't die of cold in winter or diarrhoea in summer. They die of hunger."

That was also a direct contradiction of Menem, who told Bishop Rafael Rey on Wednesday, after he remarked that letting people die of hunger was as much a crime as blocking the roads: "I haven't seen anything in the penal code about it."

Carlos Alvarez, leader of the Frepaso coalition, spoke of the need for "ethical shock-treatment" for Argentina ahead of 1999 because of the social discontent and desperation and low level of credibility in parties and politicians."
